260.title: Arjuna drops his bow
260.hook: Arjuna drops his bow and wants out; Krishna answers with karma yoga
260.carry: karma yoga: every act can be an offering
260.tomorrow: a king hears his city is on fire and says nothing of his burns. how?
260.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food before eating and dedicate their work to God in the spirit of Gita 9.27; some close a task or a meal with 'Krishnarpanam', offered to Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of the Upanishads. Your line was the silence after om is the fourth.
screen: `THE SILENCE AFTER OM IS THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Back to the battlefield. Arjuna, the finest archer of his day, stands in a chariot between two armies, with Krishna at the reins. He looks across and sees his teachers, his uncles, his cousins. His mouth goes dry. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and he sits down on the floor of the chariot. Better to live as a beggar, he says, than to do this. It's the oldest kind of wanting out: not this duty, not this family, not this day. Krishna's answer opens the first of Hinduism's three great paths.
screen: `BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `THE BOW SLIPS. HE SITS.` → `BETTER TO BEG THAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Arjuna even makes a clever argument. Krishna, you said knowing is higher than doing. So why push me into this terrible act? Krishna's answer, in chapter three of the Bhagavad Gita, is the root of karma yoga. Karma means action; yoga means joining. First: nobody gets out of acting. Not for a moment, he says. Even keeping the body alive is action. Sitting down in the chariot is a choice too. So the question isn't whether you'll act, but how. Then the key: the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna, as an offering. Yajna was the old fire sacrifice: something precious poured into the flame and never taken back. Krishna widens it to everything. Later he says it plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. That's karma yoga. Do the act as well as you can, then let it go into God's hands, like a flower set down at a shrine. It's why many Hindus offer food before eating, and why some close a task with a quiet word: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. Hindu teachers draw three great paths from the Gita: karma, the path of action; bhakti, devotion; jnana, knowledge. Arjuna's duty was a warrior's, on a terrible day. Most of us get the dishes and the night shift. The teaching doesn't ask anyone to leave the sink. It changes how you hold what's in your hands.
screen: `KARMA YOGA: THE PATH OF ACTION.` · `NOBODY GETS OUT OF ACTING.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AS AN OFFERING.` · `KRISHNARPANAM: OFFERED TO KRISHNA.` · then, large: `EVERY ACT CAN BE AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Think of the next ordinary task on your list, and picture doing it carefully, the way you'd prepare something for someone you love. Then picture setting it down like a flower at a shrine and walking away, without looking back to see who noticed. If you pray, finish it silently the way many Hindus do, Krishnarpanam, or offer it to God as you understand God; if not, offer it to the people it will help.
Karma yoga, the path of action as offering. Nobody can stop acting, Krishna tells Arjuna, so offer whatever you do.
Your line: karma yoga: every act can be an offering. Arjuna's bow is still on the chariot floor. See you tomorrow.

261.title: If Mithila burns
261.hook: a king hears his city is on fire and says nothing of his burns
261.carry: asakta: do the work, don't be owned by it
261.tomorrow: a king asks every monk: who is greater, the monk or the householder?
261.howItsDone: Janaka is remembered in Hindu tradition as the rajarshi, the king-sage who ruled fully without clinging; many Hindus end a task by offering its results to God, and Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga is still read in Vedanta societies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna dropped his bow, and Krishna answered with karma yoga. Every act can be an offering.

In that same talk, Krishna gives Arjuna an example: King Janaka, who reached perfection through action. Janaka ruled Mithila, with courts to run and people to feed, and sages honored him as a king who knew the self. The Mahabharata keeps a short song of his, and storytellers love to stage it. A messenger runs into the hall shouting that the city is on fire. Everyone leaps up. Janaka says: my wealth is endless, because nothing is mine. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
screen: `A KING WHO KNEW THE SELF.` → `THE CITY IS ON FIRE!` → `NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.`

segments.voice: Hear it the wrong way and it sounds cold: the city burns and the king shrugs. But Krishna points to Janaka for the opposite reason. Janaka and others like him reached perfection through action, he says, and then he tells Arjuna: you too should act for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the good of everyone. Janaka ran the kingdom, all of it. What he didn't do was belong to any of it. The kingdom was his work, not his self. Krishna's word for this is asakta, unattached. So, he tells Arjuna, unattached, always do the work that's yours to do. That's karma yoga's other half. Yesterday: offer the act. Today: stop owning it, and its results. Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk who gave talks in New York in the 1890s, later printed as Karma-Yoga, put it in words his listeners could carry to the office: work like a master, not a slave. The slave works for the wage and the praise, and is miserable when they don't come. The master gives the work everything, and is free either way. Non-attachment isn't caring less. Many teachers say it's what lets a person care well: a doctor who isn't owned by her pride can admit a mistake; a parent who isn't owned by the report card can still love the child who brought it home. And under it all is the Gita's teaching from chapter two: you are the atman, the self, which no weapon cuts and no fire burns. The city was never what Janaka was. Many teachers say that's how he could rule it so well.
screen: `HE REACHED PERFECTION THROUGH ACTION.` · `ACT FOR THE GOOD OF THE WORLD.` · `ASAKTA: UNATTACHED.` · `A MASTER, NOT A SLAVE.` · `NOT CARING LESS.` · `NO FIRE BURNS THE SELF.` · then, large: `DO THE WORK. DON'T BE OWNED BY IT.`

segments.voice: Think of a piece of work you're worried about, how it'll land, who'll notice. Now separate the two, the way Janaka did: the work, which is yours to do well and for others' good, and the result, which was never yours to own. Give the work your care; set the result down. If you pray, hand the result to God, as many Hindus do, with a quiet Krishnarpanam; if not, say quietly: done, and the rest isn't mine.
Asakta, unattached. Krishna: unattached, always do the work that's yours. Janaka ruled a whole kingdom that way.
Your line: asakta: do the work, don't be owned by it. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. See you tomorrow.

262.title: The birds who fed a guest
262.hook: a king asks who is greater, the monk or the householder; a family of birds answers
262.carry: grihastha: the householder's life is a path too
262.tomorrow: a proud monk burns two birds with a look. who humbles him?
262.howItsDone: In the Ramakrishna and Vedanta movements, Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read as a guide to treating ordinary work and family duty as spiritual practice, and hospitality to guests is honored in Hindu homes as a sacred duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday: King Janaka and asakta. Do the work, don't be owned by it: a master, not a slave.

Who is greater: the one who stays in the world, or the one who leaves it? The householder with a family and a mortgage, or the monk with a bowl and a road? It's an old argument. Vivekananda's New York talks kept circling back to work: his listeners' jobs, their families, their duties. In the second chapter of Karma-Yoga he takes the argument on directly. Not with a ruling. With a story about a king, a monk who said no, and a family of birds.
screen: `WHO IS GREATER?` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER, OR THE MONK?` → `A STORY, NOT A RULING.`

segments.voice: A king asked every monk who came to his court the same question: which is greater, the householder or the monk? One day a young monk said: each is great in its own place. Come, and I'll show you. In a neighboring kingdom a princess was choosing her husband before the whole court. She chose a young monk. He said no, and walked out into the forest. The king followed, lost his way, and night fell. Cold and lost, he lay down under a tree. In that tree lived a family of small birds. The father bird looked down and said: there is a guest in our house, and he's cold. He flew off and came back with a burning twig in his beak, and a fire was made. Then: our guest must be hungry, and we have nothing to give. And he dropped into the fire. His mate followed. Then their little ones. The lesson: the young man who turned down a kingdom was great as a monk. These birds were great as householders. Each is great in its own place, the chapter's title. Hindu tradition has a name for the birds' stage of life: grihastha, the householder. It's honored as the stage that feeds all the others, students, elders, monks and guests. The path isn't only for people who leave. And the Taittiriya Upanishad, in its parting words to students, says: let the guest be a god to you. The birds took it all the way.
screen: `WHO IS GREATER: HOUSEHOLDER OR MONK?` · `THE MONK WHO SAID NO.` · `THE BIRDS WHO FED A GUEST.` · `GRIHASTHA: THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH.` · then, large: `EACH IS GREAT IN ITS OWN PLACE.`

segments.voice: Let your own place come to mind, the real one: the desk, the counter, the people who need something from you this week. Breathe in and see one piece of work that's yours to do; breathe out and let it be enough of a place. If you pray, offer that one task quietly, the way the birds offered their fire; if you don't, just hold it, whole and ordinary, and rest.
Householder, in Sanskrit grihastha: one who lives in the world with a family and work. The householder and the monk can both walk the path, each great in its own place.
Your line: grihastha: the householder's life is a path too. The birds fed their guest with everything. That's day two hundred sixty-two.

263.title: The butcher who taught a monk
263.hook: a monk burns two birds with a look, and a woman at a door tells him to wait
263.carry: svadharma: your own duty, done with care, is worship
263.tomorrow: seven hundred verses later, does Arjuna pick up his bow?
263.howItsDone: Many Hindus understand caring for parents, spouse and children as dharma and as a form of worship, and the Vyadha Gita, the butcher's teaching in the Mahabharata, is often cited to show that holiness isn't tied to a particular job.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the birds who fed a guest. Grihastha: the householder's life is a path too.
screen: `EACH IS GREAT IN ITS OWN PLACE.`

segments.voice: A young monk goes into the forest and meditates for years. He gets good at it. Maybe too good. One day a crow and a crane start fighting in the branches above him, and dry leaves fall on his head. He looks up, furious, and a flash of fire leaves his eyes. The two birds fall to the ground, burned. He's thrilled: I can burn birds with a look. Then he gets hungry, walks into town, and knocks on a door to beg for food. From inside, a woman calls out: wait a little, my son. He's about to learn something the forest never taught him.
screen: `A MONK WHO BURNED TWO BIRDS.` → `A DOOR IN TOWN.` → `WAIT A LITTLE, MY SON.`

segments.voice: Vivekananda tells this story in the Karma Yoga lecture called What Is Duty? The monk stands at the door, fuming. How dare she make me wait. Doesn't she know what I can do? From inside, the woman says: don't think so much of yourself. There's no crow or crane here. He's stunned. How did she know? When she finally comes out, she explains. Her husband was ill, and she was caring for him. That was her duty, done with her whole heart, and it was all her practice. Through it, the story says, she had come to see more than his years in the forest had shown him. Then she sends him on: go to the market and find the butcher. He'll teach you. The monk is shocked: a butcher, of all people, his teacher? He goes anyway. The butcher, cutting meat, looks up: the lady sent you? Sit down, wait until I've finished. He takes the monk home, washes and feeds his old parents first, and only then sits down to teach him. What he teaches is a whole section of the Mahabharata, the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter-butcher. Vivekananda's point is sharp. The woman and the butcher were not saints by job title. Each did their svadharma, their own duty, the one in front of them, without selfishness and with care. Work done like that, he says, is worship. Fire from the eyes is not the goal.
screen: `NO CROW OR CRANE HERE.` · `SHE WAS CARING FOR HER HUSBAND.` · `THE BUTCHER WHO FED HIS PARENTS FIRST.` · `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DUTY.` · then, large: `DONE WITH CARE, IT IS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever made you wait most recently, the pharmacy line, a kid who needed one more thing, a parent on the phone, and notice the flash of heat without pushing it away. Then picture the woman at the door, doing what was in front of her. Breathe in and let the waiting be part of the work; breathe out and let the heat cool.
Vyadha, a hunter, here the butcher who taught the monk. His svadharma, done without selfishness and with care, was already his practice.
Your line: svadharma: your own duty, done with care, is worship. Whoever keeps you waiting might be caring for someone. Day two hundred sixty-three, complete.

264.title: Arjuna picks up his bow
264.hook: more than six hundred verses after he dropped it, Arjuna is ready to pick up his bow
264.tomorrow: a ghost that must be kept busy, and a dog's tail that won't stay straight
264.howItsDone: Many Hindu households offer the first portion of cooked food at the home shrine, or to a cow or birds, before the family eats, and the shrine portion is received back as prasad; the Ramakrishna Mission and many seva groups describe service to people as worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the woman at the door and the vyadha, the butcher in the market. Svadharma: your own duty, done with care, is worship.

Remember Arjuna's bow, lying on the floor of the chariot? It's still there. The armies still face each other. More than six hundred verses have passed since it slipped from his hand: almost the whole Gita, everything Krishna has taught him. And now, near the very end, Krishna asks two questions. Did you hear this with a focused mind? Is your confusion gone? Arjuna answers: my confusion is gone. My memory has come back. My doubts are gone, and I'll do as you say. The Gita doesn't stop to show his hands, but the war that follows makes it plain: he picks up the bow.
screen: `THE BOW ON THE CHARIOT FLOOR.` → `IS YOUR CONFUSION GONE?` → `HE PICKS IT UP.`

segments.voice: What changed his mind? Not a new job. Same battlefield, same duty. What changed is how he holds it. A little earlier in chapter eighteen of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives the line karma yoga leans on more than almost any other. Paraphrased: the one from whom all beings come, by whom all this is spread out, worshiping that one with your own work, a person reaches perfection. Svakarmana tam abhyarcya. With your own work, worship. Not someone else's work. Not a holy job you'll get around to someday. Your own. You can see it in a lot of Hindu kitchens. The first roti off the pan, or the first spoon of rice, goes on a little plate before the family's shrine, or to the cow outside, or to the birds. Nobody thinks the gods are starving. The cooking itself has been offered, and what was set before the shrine is taken back as prasad, a blessing. Then everyone eats. Vivekananda carried this into the street: serve people as you'd serve God, because God is in them. That became the heart of the Ramakrishna Mission, which he founded in 1897. And chapter two says what offered work looks like from outside: yoga is skill in action. Offered work isn't sloppy work with a holy feeling. It's careful. Nobody offers a burnt roti on purpose.

segments.voice: Picture the first real task waiting for you after this, your hands on the keyboard, the wheel, the dishes or the lesson plan, and notice how you usually meet it: rushed, bored, braced. Now picture doing that same task with care, as if someone you love were going to receive it. If you pray, dedicate it silently, the way the first roti goes to the shrine; if you don't, just let it be done well, for its own sake.
Svakarmana, with one's own work. Krishna's last word on karma yoga: with your own work, worship. Offered work is careful work.
Your line: with your own work, worship. Arjuna picked up his bow. Two hundred sixty-four days, and counting.

265.title: The ghost and the curly tail
265.hook: a ghost, a dog's curly tail, and why seva still matters when the world won't change
265.carry: seva: serving others changes the one who serves
265.tomorrow: a mongoose, half gold, says a king's great sacrifice isn't enough. why?
265.howItsDone: In seva, service offered freely, many Hindus aim to help without clinging to results or credit, often using the Gita's image of the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna picked up his bow. With your own work, worship; offered work is careful work.

A year of volunteering, donating, showing up for the cause, and the problem looks exactly the same. The shelter is still full. The inbox is still full. And a quiet voice asks: what's the point? Vivekananda took that question seriously. In his Karma Yoga lectures he answered it with a strange little story about a man, a ghost, and a dog's tail that would not stay straight. The chapter's title sounds almost rude: We Help Ourselves, Not the World.
screen: `THE PROBLEM LOOKS THE SAME.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Vivekananda tells it. A man wanted a ghost to do his work for him, and he got one. But there was a catch: the ghost had to be kept busy every minute, or it would kill him. It finished every job in no time. Build a house: done. Clear a field: done. The man, terrified, ran to a wise teacher, who said: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail. The ghost pulled the tail straight. Let go, and it curled back up. Pulled again. Curled. That kept it busy. The world, Vivekananda said, is like that dog's tail. People keep pulling it straight; let go, and it curls. So is helping pointless? No. That's the turn. When we help, he said, we're not fixing the world. The world will go on. We are the ones being changed. So, he said, be grateful to the person you help: they gave you the chance. Hindus call this kind of help seva, selfless service, and many temples run on it. And serve, he said, like a master, not a slave, the way Janaka ruled. The Gita has a picture for it: the one who acts, offering the action and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by it, the way a lotus leaf sits in water and stays dry. The tail still curls. You keep straightening it anyway, and you stay dry.
screen: `A GHOST THAT MUST BE KEPT BUSY.` · `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.` · `SEVA: THE HELPER IS THE ONE WHO CHANGES.` · `A LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `SEVA CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back: a cause, a messy house, a relative who won't change. Breathe in and feel how much you want the result; breathe out and set the result down beside you, just for now. Then picture doing the next small piece anyway, because it's worth doing, like the lotus leaf: in the water, and dry.
Master, one who works freely, not for reward. In seva, we help ourselves, not the world: the work changes the worker. Stay dry like the lotus leaf.
Your line: seva: serving others changes the one who serves. The tail still curls, and the helper still grows. Day two hundred sixty-five, done.

266.title: The half-golden mongoose
266.hook: a mongoose, half gold, rolls through a king's great sacrifice and says it isn't enough
266.carry: dana: a gift is weighed by what it costs
266.tomorrow: the second road: what is bhakti, the path of love?
266.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often retell the Mahabharata's story of the half-golden mongoose to explain that the worth of a gift, a sacrifice or a day's work lies in how freely and fully it's given, not in its size.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghost and the dog's curly tail taught seva: serving others changes the one who serves. Today, the last day of karma yoga.
screen: `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.`

segments.voice: The great war of the Mahabharata is over. The winner, King Yudhishthira, holds an enormous sacrifice to mark his reign: gold for the priests, food for the crowds, gifts on every side. Then, in the middle of the ceremony, a mongoose runs in. Half its body is ordinary brown fur. The other half shines like gold. It rolls on the ground, gets up, looks at itself, and says: this great sacrifice isn't equal to a little barley flour once given by a poor family. Everyone goes quiet. What family? What flour?
screen: `A KING'S GREAT SACRIFICE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR.`

segments.voice: The mongoose tells them. There was a famine. A poor brahmin lived with his wife, his son and his son's wife, and for days they'd had nothing. At last they got a little barley flour, just enough for four small portions. They were about to eat when a guest came to the door, starving. The father gave his portion. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. The guest ate, and revealed himself: he was Dharma, the god of righteousness himself, and he blessed them. The mongoose had come out of its hole and rolled in the few grains left on the floor, and wherever the flour touched, it turned to gold. Ever since, it's gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, rolling on the ground, looking for another gift that great, to turn the other half gold. It still hasn't found one. Vivekananda retold this story in his talks on karma yoga. The point isn't that kings shouldn't give. It's how Hindus weigh dana, giving: not by its price, but by what it costs the one who gives, and how freely it's given. That's where the week has been going. Arjuna's dropped bow: every act an offering. Janaka: unattached. The birds and the butcher, each great in their own place. Your own work as worship. And now: the smallest gift, fully given, outweighing gold.
screen: `FOUR PORTIONS OF BARLEY FLOUR.` · `EACH ONE GIVEN TO A GUEST.` · `THE GRAINS THAT TURNED TO GOLD.` · `DANA: WEIGHED BY WHAT IT COSTS.` · then, large: `A GIFT IS WEIGHED BY WHAT IT COSTS.`

segments.voice: Look back over the week and let each picture pass with a breath: the bow on the chariot floor, the city on fire, the birds and their fire, the butcher feeding his parents, the first roti, the curly tail, the mongoose. Then ask: what's one small thing I gave this week that nobody saw? Don't grade it, just notice it was given; if you pray, offer the whole week as it was, and if not, rest in it.
Saktu, barley flour, the poor family's whole gift. Dana, giving, is weighed by what it costs the giver and how freely it's given. Small gifts can outweigh gold.
Your line: dana: a gift is weighed by what it costs. Tomorrow, a new road: devotion. That's the karma week, finished.
